SUMMARY
STAT3 is an oncogenic transcription factor that activates cancer cell signaling and induces an immunosuppressive immune environment, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Transcription factors are exceptionally challenging targets and there are no Food and Drug Administration-approved STAT3 inhibitors. We previously reported positive pharmacodynamics of a linear STAT3 decoy oligonucleotide administered intratumorally in a Phase 0 trial in patients with head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Here, we describe the anti-tumor and immune effects of a systemically administered cyclic STAT3 decoy (CS3D) in immunocompetent HNSCC murine models and the safety and efficacy of CS3D in a clinical trial in pet cats with HNSCC. Responders in the clinical trial (35% disease control rate) showed significant differences in selected peripheral blood immune parameters as well as elevated PD-1 expression in the tumors compared with non-responders. These findings support a clinical trial of CS3D in HNSCC patients.

INTRODUCTION
Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is an oncogenic transcription factor that is hyperactivated in most solid tumors and hematopoietic malignancies. Its role in stimulating tumor cell proliferation/survival, inducing immunosuppression, and promoting cancer drug resistance makes STAT3 a particularly attractive therapeutic target for most cancers.
1
–
5
Like all transcription factors, STAT3 has long been considered an exceptionally challenging target due to its intracellular localization and lack of enzymatic activity. To address the gap in clinical STAT3 inhibitors, we designed a 15-bp duplex oligonucleotide with free ends, termed the STAT3 decoy, which resembles a STAT3 response element, binds selectively to activated STAT3, competitively inhibits STAT3 binding to target gene promoters, induces head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) apoptosis, and suppresses xenograft tumor growth.
4
,
6
–
10
A Phase 0 clinical trial
11
involving intratumoral injection of the STAT3 decoy in human HNSCC patients undergoing surgical resection with curative intent demonstrated downmodulation of STAT3 target genes in resected tumors after a single injection.
12
A cyclic version of the STAT3 decoy exhibits improved thermal stability and nuclease resistance, and inhibited the growth of xenograft tumors following systemic delivery in immunodeficient mice.
12
–
15
The impact of cyclic STAT3 decoy (CS3D) administration on the immune system has not been studied, limiting the design of further clinical trials with this promising anti-cancer agent. An antisense oligonucleotide targeting STAT3 mRNA (AZD9150, danvatirsen) has shown safety and activity in early phase studies in lymphoma and lung cancer where it reversed a suppressive tumor microenvironment and promoted proinflammatory gene expression changes in patient tumors.
16
,
17
Cumulative evidence underscores the importance of the immune system in HNSCC progression.
18
–
22
In the present study, we tested the CS3D in multiple different preclinical HNSCC models (murine and feline cell lines, organoids containing immune components, and immunocompetent xenograft tumors) and found evidence of dose-dependent anti-tumor activity. Depletion of CD8
+
T-cells reversed the anti-tumor effects
in vivo
, strongly implicating the impact of the STAT3 decoy on the tumor microenvironment.
While testing novel anti-cancer agents in both immunodeficient and immunocompetent mouse models of cancer can demonstrate anti-tumor mechanisms, these models do not reflect the heterogeneity of spontaneously arising malignancies. Naturally occurring tumors in pet animals provide an opportunity to test novel cancer therapeutics and validate preclinical findings. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is commonly diagnosed in pet cats, is locally aggressive, and considered incurable.
23
,
24
Feline oral cancer is generally fatal within 2 to 3 months and radiation treatment provides only a modest survival benefit.
25
–
27
There is remarkable clinical, histopathologic, and immunologic similarity between feline and human HNSCC.
23
,
24
,
28
–
30
Both species have similar environmental exposures, genetic and biologic diversity, and mature immune systems. Human and feline HNSCCs are both naturally occurring and heterogeneous and feline tumors exhibit similar expression and mutational profiles of key biomarkers, including EGFR, VEGF, p16, p53, and Rb.
23
,
24
,
28
,
29
,
31
–
35
Hyperactivation of STAT3, as assessed by phosphorylation, has also been reported in 48% of feline HNSCC tumors.
36
Because of the similarities between human and feline HNSCC, we sought to study the biologic effects of the CS3D in pet cats who develop HNSCC to inform the design of future human trials and identify biomarkers. A total of twenty cats were enrolled and treated on a Phase I protocol. There was no evidence of a dose-limiting toxicity even at the highest dose tested (10 mg/kg). Using RECIST criteria
37
, two cats experienced partial tumor responses and five cats demonstrated stable disease while the remaining thirteen cats showed tumor progression for an overall disease control rate of 35%. Correlative biomarker studies including RNAseq analysis of the tumor biopsies and flow cytometry of the peripheral blood demonstrated distinct differences between responding and non-responding cats in their tumor gene expression profiles as well as circulating immune cell populations.
These cumulative findings suggest that treatment with this first-in-class STAT3 inhibitor is safe and may be an effective anti-cancer strategy, exerting its effects on both tumor and immune cells. Further clinical testing in both companion animals and human patients with cancer is warranted.
RESULTS
Cyclic STAT3 decoy (CS3D) reduces cell viability and the levels of STAT3 target genes in murine HNSCC cell lines
We previously reported that intravenous administration of CS3D inhibits the growth of human HNSCC cell line-derived xenograft tumors in immunodeficient mice.
12
,
13
Because genetic inactivation of the
STAT3
gene in immune cells promotes anti-tumor immunity,
38
–
44
we sought to determine the impact of the CS3D in well-characterized immunocompetent murine models of HNSCC prior to conducting clinical evaluation of CS3D in pet cats. MOC1, MOC22, and mEER are murine HNSCC cell lines that grow well as tumors in immunocompetent, syngeneic C57BL/6 mice and represent both human papilloma virus (HPV)-negative (MOC1, MOC22) and HPV-positive (mEER) HNSCC.
45
–
49
We first examined the impact of CS3D on the viability of MOC1, MOC22, and mEER
in vitro
(
Figure 1A
). As controls, cells were left untreated or were treated with Lipofectamine alone, or with Lipofectamine plus a scrambled sequence version of the cyclic decoy (SCR). Treatment of each cell line with 1 μM CS3D resulted in a roughly 40-60% loss of cell viability after 48 hours. By contrast, treatment with 1 μM SCR resulted in less than a 10% loss of cell viability. To confirm the inhibitory impact of CS3D on the expression of STAT3 target genes in the murine HNSCC cell lines, we analyzed the expression of three representative target genes (
VEGF, CCND1, Bcl-X
L
) 24 hours after treatment with CS3D or SCR (1 μM). In all three cell lines, treatment with CS3D resulted in a statistically significant reduction in
VEGF, CCND1
, and
Bcl-X

Figure 1B
). An exception to this was
CCND1
mRNA in MOC1 where expression only trended downward with CS3D treatment (p = 0.079). Collectively, these results show that CS3D reduced cell viability and the expression of STAT3 target genes and in both HPV-negative and HPV-positive murine HNSCC cell line models.

CS3D inhibits growth and ATP production in murine HNSCC tumor organoids
We next sought to determine the impact of CS3D treatment on murine HNSCC models grown
ex vivo
and retaining 3-dimensional (3D) tumor architecture and associated tumor-infiltrating immune cells. For this purpose, MOC1, MOC22, and mEER cells were grown as subcutaneous tumors in immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice and excised tumor tissues containing both tumor epithelial cells and immune cells were embedded in collagen gels and used to generate organoids using the air-liquid interface (ALI) method.
50
A fourth murine HNSCC model, 4MOSC1, derived from C57BL/6 mice,
51
was also incorporated in these studies. After 7 days of culture, we successfully generated organoids from all 4 murine HNSCC tumor models. Comparison of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained organoid sections with H&E-stained sections of the corresponding primary tumors demonstrated that the organoids retained architectural similarity with the original primary tumors (
Figure 2A
–
D
). The organoids exhibited a keratinizing, well-to-moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma morphology and a mild inflammatory infiltrate (
Figure 2A
–
D
,
Supplementary Figure S1
). Immunofluorescence staining demonstrated the expression of E-cadherin-positive tumor-associated epithelial cells, vimentin-positive fibroblasts, and CD45-positive immune cells in both the organoids and the primary tumors from which the organoids were derived (
Supplementary Figure S1
).

Hence, CS3D inhibited the growth of the murine HNSCC models in both 2D cultures and 3D cultures containing immune components derived from the primary tumors.
CS3D inhibits the growth of murine HNSCC tumors in immunocompetent mice
CS3D has been shown to inhibit the growth of human tumor xenografts in immunodeficient mice.
12
,
13
,
15
Here, we tested the impact of CS3D treatment on the growth of murine HNSCC tumors in immunocompetent mice in 3 different models (
Figure 3
). MOC22, mEER, and 4MOSC1 were grown as subcutaneous tumors in the flanks of syngeneic, wild-type C57BL/6 mice. We elected to implant the cells subcutaneously since studies assessing the growth of murine orthotopic (buccal or floor-of-mouth) HNSCC tumors are limited by the morbidity of oral tumors on the ability of the mouse to eat, thereby creating a very narrow window to study therapeutic effects. In addition, others have observed similar kinetics of immune infiltration in subcutaneously and orthotopically implanted immunocompetent oral cancer cells.
52
Tumor-bearing mice were randomized for treatment with vehicle (saline), SCR (10 mg/kg), or CS3D (5 or 10 mg/kg), 5 times/week via tail vein intravenous delivery. The concentrations of CS3D chosen for use were based on pilot dose-response data in human HNSCC xenografts. Treatment of the MOC22 model with CS3D resulted in potent, dose-dependent inhibition of tumor growth, with complete inhibition seen with the 10 mg/kg dose (
Figure 3A
). Inhibition of MOC22 tumor growth was associated with induction of apoptosis, as demonstrated by immunoblotting of tumor lysates for cleavage of PARP protein (
Supplementary Figure S2A
). Similar dose-dependent inhibition of tumor growth was observed with the mEER model, although the 10 mg/kg CS3D dose was somewhat less effective than in MOC22 tumors (
Figure 3B
). In the 4MOSC1 model, only the 5 mg/kg dose of CS3D was tested, where partial inhibition of tumor growth was seen (
Figure 3C
). By contrast, in all three murine HNSCC models treatment with the scrambled cyclic decoy, SCR, had no impact on tumor growth. Inhibition of murine HNSCC tumor growth
in vivo
by CS3D was associated with reduced expression of the STAT3 target genes
VEGF, CCND1
, and
Bcl-X
L
(
Supplementary Figure S2B
), similar to what was observed
in vitro
(
Figure 1B
). Additionally, immunoblotting of pre-treatment tumor lysates for tyrosine (Y705)-phosphorylated STAT3 (p-STAT3), the activated form, revealed similar levels of p-STAT3 in the most responsive tumor model (MOC22) and the less responsive models (mEER, 4MOSC1)(
Supplementary Figure S2C
). Thus, there was no clear evidence of a correlation between p-STAT3 expression levels and response to CS3D in these murine models of HNSCC.

Our results demonstrated that CS3D treatment inhibited the growth of HNSCC tumors in immunocompetent mice and raised the question whether immune cells contributed to these anti-tumor effects. CD8-positive (CD8
+
) T-cells are major effectors of anti-tumor immunity and activation of STAT3 in tumor infiltrating CD8
+
inhibits the activity of these cells. Therefore, we investigated the role of CD8
+
cells in the anti-tumor activity of CS3D by performing an immunodepletion experiment (
Figure 3D
&
3E
). C57BL/6 mice harboring MOC22 tumors were first given intraperitoneal injections of anti-CD8 or anti-IgG control (0.5 mg/mouse/dose) on 3 consecutive days. Twenty-four hours after the third dose, two mice from each group were sacrificed and their spleens and tumors were harvested for flow cytometric analysis of CD8
+
cells. Relative to mice treated with anti-IgG, mice treated with anti-CD8 exhibited a 95% or greater reduction in CD8
+
spleen cells and a 94% or greater reduction in tumor CD8
+
cells, demonstrating efficient depletion of this immune cell population (
Figure 3D
). Of the remaining mice, half in each group (anti-CD8 and anti-IgG groups) were then treated with CS3D (10 mg/kg, 5 times/week) and the other half were treated with SCR at the same dose and schedule. As shown in
Figure 3E
, treatment with anti-CD8 had no effect on tumor growth in mice receiving SCR. By contrast, treatment with anti-CD8 inhibited the anti-tumor effects of CS3D administration. Hence, in the MOC22 model the anti-tumor activity of intravenously administered CS3D appears to be largely mediated by CD8
+
immune cells.
Because the CS3D molecule contains a single CpG sequence, a potential ligand for Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9), we considered the possibility that CS3D activation of anti-tumor immunity was due to CS3D activation of TLR9. To test this possibility, we employed TLR9-expressing human monocytic THP-1 cells engineered to express reporter constructs for NF-κB or interferon regulatory factor (IRF), downstream signaling molecules that are activated when TLR9 signaling is activated. Treatment of these cells with 5 μM of a CpG-containing positive control oligonucleotide (ODN-pos) resulted in marked activation of NF-κB and IRF, whereas treatment with 5 μM of a negative control oligonucleotide (ODN-neg) lacking CpG motifs failed to activate these signaling molecules (
Figure 3F
and
3G
). Importantly, treatment with CS3D at 1, 5, or 20 μM also failed to activate TLR9. Thus, the anti-tumor effects of CS3D likely do not involve CS3D activation of TLR9.
Additional studies examined whether treatment with CS3D induced a durable anti-tumor response. Mice harboring MOC22 tumors were treated with vehicle or CS3D for a period of 19 days, followed by discontinuation of all treatments (
Supplementary Figure S2D
). Tumors were observed to regrow after cessation of CS3D treatment, indicating that the anti-tumor activity of CS3D monotherapy requires continued treatment in this model.
Treatments combining CS3D with other conventional or molecular targeting agents are potentially promising. We previously reported enhanced anti-tumor efficacy when the first-generation (noncyclic) STAT3 decoy was combined with cisplatin
in vitro
and
in vivo
.
53
Here, we performed preliminary studies to test the impact of CS3D in combination with the FDA-approved EGFR monoclonal antibody cetuximab, a mainstay molecular targeting agent for HNSCC, against human HNSCC xenograft tumors grown in immunodeficient mice (
Supplementary Figure S3
). Treatment with CS3D plus cetuximab resulted in significantly enhanced anti-tumor activity relative to either agent alone, with potent tumor regression occurring following treatment with the combination. This supports the testing of CS3D in combination with other agents currently used in the treatment of HNSCC.
CS3D inhibits the growth of feline HNSCC cells
Immunocompetent murine HNSCC models do not arise spontaneously and reflect few of the biologic underpinnings of human cancer. We and others have reported on the similarity of spontaneously-arising feline oral cancer to human HPV-negative disease.
23
,
24
,
28
,
29
,
31
–
33
,
36
Feline oral cancer is universally fatal with no effective treatments.
28
,
54
Prior to initiating a clinical trial of CS3D treatment in pet cats with oral cancer we investigated the impact of CS3D on the feline oral cancer cell lines SCCF2 and SCCF3.
55
Immunoblotting confirmed that both cell lines express readily detectable p-STAT3 and total STAT3, consistent with a prior report (
Figure 4A
).
36
Treatment of SCCF2 and SCCF3 cells with CS3D resulted in inhibition of cell survival relative to controls (
Figure 4B
), demonstrating CS3D biological activity in feline HNSCC cells and supporting clinical evaluation of CS3D in pet cats with oral cancer.

Cyclic STAT3 decoy is well tolerated and exhibits anti-tumor efficacy in pet cats with oral cancer
The safety and maximum tolerated dose of CS3D was next evaluated in a Phase I clinical trial in pet cats with biopsy-confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity (
Figure 5A
). A standard 3 + 3 dose escalation scheme was conducted using dose cohorts of 2.5 mg/kg, 5.0 mg/kg, 7.5 mg/kg, and 10.0 mg/kg. The doses selected were based on the intratumoral concentrations delivered in our earlier human phase 0 study of the noncyclic STAT3 decoy.
12
Dose escalation proceeded with 3 cats enrolled in each of the 4 dose cohorts (
Table 1
). No dose limiting adverse events were observed. An additional 8 cats were enrolled after dose escalation resulting in a total of 11 cats receiving 10 mg/kg of CS3D. Cats were enrolled on the trial with a planned duration of 29 days, and intravenous injections of CS3D planned on days 1, 3, and 5 in week 1, and weekly thereafter on days 8, 15, and 22, for a total of 6 doses.

Twenty cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma that met inclusion criteria were enrolled in the study. The characteristics of the cats and their tumors are summarized in

The median maximum tumor diameter at study enrollment was 2.3 cm (range, 1.1-8.7 cm;

Twelve cats developed mild, non-dose limiting anemia during the study period. Anemia in 7 of these cats was classified as grade 1 and in 5 cats as grade 2. Two of the cats that developed grade 2 anemia progressed from grade 1 anemia present at study enrollment. All anemias were non-regenerative and did not require clinical intervention. No other adverse events occurred during the study period that were attributable to CS3D.
We previously reported lack of toxicity of the CS3D in mice at doses up to 100 mg/kg.

Given the paucity of adverse events we observed in the feline cancer patients, we performed formal toxicology testing in rats with repeated systemic administration of the CS3D up to 500 mg/kg with no evidence of dose limiting toxicities (DLTs), as assessed by body weights, food consumption, or hematologic and urinalysis parameters (
Supplementary Figure S4
and data not shown). ADZ9150 (danvatirsen) is an antisense oligonucleotide targeting STAT3 that is being tested in HNSCC patients. It is noteworthy that the administration of this chemically modified antisense oligonucleotide is limited by thrombocytopenia.

DISCUSSION
STAT3 has been widely reported to both drive cancer cell proliferation/survival and tumor growth as well as contribute to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in many solid tumors and hematopoietic malignancies. Long considered an exceptionally challenging target, a variety of natural products and inhibitors of upstream receptor and non-receptor kinases have been tested as putative STAT3 inhibitors in preclinical models and human cancer patients. Several agents have advanced to early phase clinical testing, most notably an antisense oligonucleotide (AZD9150 or danvatirsen) and the small molecule TTI-101. Danvatirsen, which targets STAT3 mRNA and reduces STAT3 protein expression, is currently in clinical development for HNSCC, alone and in combination with immunotherapy (
NCT05814666
;
NCT02499328
). The impact of danvatirsen in human cancer patients has been reported to be substantially exerted via effects on immune cells.
16
,
17
,
67
We tested a murine version of danvatirsen (mAZD9150) in a murine HNSCC preclinical model and observed downregulation of STAT3 and the STAT3 target gene encoding cyclin D1, but negligible anti-tumor activity (
Supplementary Figure S7
). TTI-101 targets the SH2 domain of STAT3 and acts to block recruitment of STAT3 to activated cytokine receptors as well as dimerization of the STAT3 protein, thereby preventing STAT3 activation.
68
,
69
A Phase I trial of TTI-101 in human cancer patients with advanced solid tumors (
NCT03195699
), albeit not including HNSCC, demonstrated good tolerability, with partial responses or stable disease in 12% and 41%, respectively, of 41 evaluable pateints.
70
Taking a different approach, we designed a decoy oligonucleotide mimicking the STAT3 response element sequence (as found in the c-
fos
gene) that binds and inhibits active STAT3 (p-STAT3) and demonstrated anti-tumor efficacy in HNSCC cell lines and immunodeficient xenograft models.
4
,
6
,
8
,
10
,
53
Other groups validated the impact of this first-generation, linear, decoy molecule in a variety of additional preclinical models including cancers of the breast, ovaries, colon, skin, liver, lung, esophagus, and brain.
71
–
79
We completed a Phase 0 clinical trial in human HNSCC patients and found that administration of the STAT3 decoy resulted in decreased tumor target gene expression compared with saline injected control tumors.
12
The first-generation decoy was limited by thermal and enzymatic instability due to free ends of the double-stranded molecule and thus required intratumoral administration. To address these barriers to clinical development, we generated a more stable drug by adding hexaethylene glycolyl linkers and cyclizing the molecule.
12
Systemic administration of this second-generation decoy, the CS3D, inhibited the growth of HNSCC and lung cancer xenograft tumors in immunodeficient mice and has also been reported to show activity in preventing carcinogen-induced lung cancer development.
12
,
13
,
15
,
80
,
81
In view of the immunosuppressive impact of STAT3 activation in the tumor microenvironment, in the present study, we tested the anti-tumor and immune effects of the CS3D in several immunocompetent HNSCC models. Treatment with CS3D inhibited cellular viabilities and expression of STAT3 target genes in the murine HNSCC cell lines and also inhibited the growth of three dimensional HNSCC organoids, reflecting the biologic potency of this agent and justifying further
in vivo
testing.
The
in vivo
anti-tumor effects of the CS3D were tested in three immunocompetent HNSCC settings including an HPV-positive (mEER) and two HPV-negative (MOC22 and 4MOSC1) models. Systemic administration of the CS3D significantly inhibited tumor growth in all three models. Because we did not use a metastatic murine model and metastasis was not assessed in the cats with oral cancer, we cannot draw conclusions regarding potential anti-metastatic properties of CS3D. The importance of immune cells for the anti-tumor effects of CS3D in the murine models was confirmed by CD8 depletion, thus confirming an impact of the CS3D on both the cancer cells and immune cells in the tumor microenvironment
in vivo
. Others have reported that myeloid cell-targeted STAT3 inhibition sensitizes HNSCC cells to radiotherapy and T-cell-mediated immunity.
82
Collectively, these findings support an anti-tumor effect of targeted STAT3 inhibition in both immune cells and HNSCC tumor cells.
Testing of novel agents in human cancer patients requires completion of FDA IND-directed pharmacokinetic and toxicology studies before first-in-human administration can be initiated. To better inform the design of a future Phase 1 human trial, we sought to test the safety and preliminary efficacy in pet animals who develop HNSCC. Squamous cell carcinomas of the oral cavity that closely resemble human HNSCC are commonly diagnosed in both dogs and cats.
24
,
30
While most dogs are large enough to be able to tolerate an oral cavity/jaw resection, cats cannot survive such surgeries. Oral cancer arises in about five out of every thousand cats and accounts for approximately 10% of all feline cancers. Feline oral cancer is locally aggressive, generally resistant to chemotherapy, and uniformly lethal, even with palliative radiation. Further, feline HNSCC is characterized by heterogeneous tumor populations that mimic advanced, HPV-negative HNSCC in humans.
29
,
31
–
34
,
36
,
54
The performance of clinical trials in companion animals (dogs and cats) with cancer offers the opportunity to test novel agents in large animals with spontaneously arising tumors (similar to human cancer) which serves as the basis for the NCI comparative oncology clinical trials program (
https://ccr.cancer.gov/comparative-oncology-program
).
We first confirmed a high sequence homology between the human and cat STAT3 response element from the c-
fos
gene (100% identical over the 15-bp represented in the CS3D). We then validated the impact of the CS3D in immortalized cell lines developed from feline oral cancer and previously reported to be sensitive to a preclinical STAT3 pathway inhibitor.
34
,
36
Next, we initiated an IACUC-approved Phase I clinical trial in pet cats with oral cancer referred to the University of California Davis Veterinary Hospital. Of the twenty cats enrolled and treated on the trial, seven exhibited either a partial response or stable disease during the 29-day study period, reflecting a disease control rate of 35%. While survival was not a primary endpoint, the seven cats who experienced stable disease or a partial response during the study period survived significantly longer that the cats who experienced progressive disease (median of 57 days in non-responders compared with 161 days in responders). There was no evidence of a dose-response in the responders. It is noteworthy that this is the only STAT3 inhibitor that has been tested in cats with HNSCC.
We previously reported the immune cell markers that characterize feline HNSCC.
29
In an effort to identify immune biomarkers, peripheral blood was collected from all subjects prior to initiating treatment on day 1 and prior to administration of subsequent weekly doses after administration of the 3
rd
dose of the CS3D. We found that the Ki67
+
population of regulatory CD4
+
T-cell subsets (FoxP3
+
and CD25
+
FoxP3
+
) was significantly reduced on the final day of collection in responders compared with non-responders. In addition, the total frequency of CD4
−
CD8
−
T-cells was significantly lower for the responder cohort on both day 1 and the final day, suggesting potential predictive biomarkers in conjunction with immunomodulation. Notably, sparse PCA analysis using T-cell subsets discriminated between the responding and non-responding cohorts. Moreover, responders exhibited a significantly lower N/L ratio compared with non-responders, consistent with reports demonstrating that a low N/L ratio is a positive prognostic indicator in human HNSCC.
63
–
65
We previously reported decreased expression of Bcl-X
L
, the product of a known STAT3 target gene, in human HNSCC tumors several hours after a single intratumoral injection of the earlier, linear version of the STAT3 decoy.
12
Here, we found that a majority of the cats demonstrated downregulation of Bcl-X
L
protein after receiving three intravenous doses of the CS3D during the first week of therapy, suggesting an on-target effect of the drug. Unexpectedly, we found that baseline p-STAT3 expression was inversely correlated with responders compared with non-responders. Further studies are needed to elucidate the precise mechanism of this potential predictive biomarker.
It should be noted that our analyses of immune cell populations in cats were limited by the availability of antibodies cross-reactive with feline antigens. This paucity of feline-reactive antibodies prevented detailed investigation of certain unexpected findings. In particular, we unexpectedly observed that responding cats exhibited a trend towards lower baseline levels of Ki67
+
/CD25
−
FoxP3
−
CD4
+
T-cells, a population of cells that might be proliferating effector memory T-cells. However, a definitive functional description of this population as proliferating effector memory T-cells would require assessment of additional memory markers (e.g. CD45RO, CD45RA, CCR7, CD62L, or CD127), and antibodies against such markers were not available.
Collectively, our findings suggest an association between clinical impact and immunomodulation by the CS3D. Tumor tissue was also harvested on days 1 and 8. Among the genes upregulated in responders on day 8 was the gene encoding PD-1. Given the widespread use of anti-PD-1 agents in human HNSCC for both recurrent/metastatic disease and newly diagnosed, locally advanced cancer, this finding supports further testing of the CS3D in combination with FDA-approved immune checkpoint inhibitors including pembrolizumab and nivolumab as the CS3D is clinically advanced.

In the current study we also generated a scrambled sequence cyclic decoy (SCR) that retained the overall cyclic structure but comprised a scrambled nucleotide sequence. CS3D and SCR were first synthesized as linear molecules, then subjected to ligation to generate the cyclic form. ™

TL (Sigma-Aldrich) for 15 minutes with gentle mixing in a tube rotator to dissociate organoids into single cells. ®

Briefly, sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated through graded alcohols, treated with proteinase K, and incubated to quench endogenous peroxidase activity. Stained slides were examined using a brightfield microscope, and two representative areas per tumor were selected and imaged at 40X magnification. Image analysis was performed using QuPath software. RNAseq
Tumor punch biopsies (4 mm) were obtained from pet cats in the clinical trial on day 1 (pre-treatment) and on day 8 prior to the day 8 treatment with CS3D. Samples were immediately frozen and stored at −80° C until batch preparation of RNA. RNA was extracted using the Direct-zol RNA Miniprep kit (Zymo Research) according to the manufacturer’s modified protocol for “RNA purification from the aqueous phase after Tri Reagent extraction”. Briefly, tumor samples were crushed in liquid nitrogen, mixed with 500μL Trizol, and further lysed using a bead mill. Chloroform (100 μL) was added to the lysate, mixed well, and the mixture subjected to centrifugation. The aqueous phase was removed, mixed with an equal volume of 100% ethanol and added to a Zymo-Spin IICR column. After centrifugation and a quick wash, on-column DNA digestion was performed, followed by additional washes. Total RNA was eluted with 50 μL of RNAse/DNAse-free water and 1 μg was submitted to Novogene Co. (Sacramento, CA) for quality testing, library prep, and sequencing.
RNA quantification, integrity and purity were assessed on an Agilent 5400 analyzer. All samples passed quality control (RIN values ranged from 4.0-8.7). Messenger RNA was purified from total RNA using poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads. After fragmentation, first strand cDNA was synthesized using random hexamer primers, followed by non-directional library preparation using the NEBNext Ultra II RNA Library Prep kit (New England Biolabs). The library was checked with a Qubit dsDNA HS assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and real-time PCR for quantification, and an Agilent 5400 bioanalyzer for size distribution. Quantified libraries were pooled and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 PE150 sequencer.
Analysis of RNAseq data:
Raw data (raw reads) of fastq format were first processed with fastp software. In this step, clean data were obtained by removing reads containing adapters, reads containing poly-A and low-quality reads. Further steps were based on the clean data. Paired-end clean reads were aligned to the reference genome Felis_catus_9.0 using Hisat2 v2.0.5.
89
This tool was chosen because it can generate a database of splice junctions based on the gene model annotation and therefore generate a better mapping result than other non-splice mapping tools. FeatureCounts v1.5.0-p3
90
was used to count the reads numbers mapped to each gene.
Statistical Analysis
For preclinical studies involving treatment of cell lines or mouse models of HNSCC with CS3D, SCR, or mutant CS3D, data were analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by ad hoc pairwise comparisons with contrasts. The multiplicity of ad hoc comparisons was controlled using Sidak’s method.
83
To satisfy the assumptions of ANOVA, data were log-transformed when necessary. Tumor volume data were also analyzed on the log-transformed scale.
For specimens from the clinical trial, to test for differences in immune cell subsets between responder and non-responder patient cohorts at selected time points, a two-tailed Mann Whitney
U
-test was performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Prism version 10.3). Graphs describing immune cell subsets frequencies were generated in GraphPad Prism. Log transformed fold-changes in subset frequencies between day 1 (baseline) and day 8 (following initial three treatments) were analyzed for the clinical cohorts (responders and non-responders) one subset at a time by a linear mixed effects model followed by a contrast for fold-changes between responders and non-responders, using R project for statistical computing software.
91
The mixed effects model accounted for correlation between day 1 and day 8 measurements within the study subjects. The significance of the contrasts was assessed while inflation in the type I error due to repeated comparisons of responders versus non-responders across multiple cell subtypes was controlled by the Bonferroni method. To identify a group of cell subsets that collectively distinguish responders from non-responders, Sparse Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed, using R “sparsepca” Package. PCA is a dimension reduction technique that summarizes the information content of a large dataset into a smaller set of uncorrelated variables known as principal components. Sparse PCA is a version of PCA that uses a reduced number of variables to build principal components to avoid overfitting and improve interpretability.
92
The first three principal components found in the unsupervised Sparse PCA of immune cell subset frequency data were tested for their ability to separate responders from non-responders via a two-sample t-test on their respective component scores. Principal component scores denote the locations of each feline clinical trial patient in the new coordinate system defined by the respective principal components.
For analysis of RNAseq data, processing of the expression counts was performed using the edgeR R package.
93
Library size was adjusted with the calcNormFactors function.
94
Raw counts were transformed into log counts per million using the voom function. Then differential expression was estimated using the limma-voom method.
95
This analysis led to a p-value for every gene for the null hypothesis of no change in mean expression. The Benjamini-Hochberg method was used to adjust for multiple comparisons, and an associated False Discovery Rate<0.01 was the cutoff for differential expression. Genes were ranked by −log(p-value) * sign(logFoldChange). To identify overrepresented pathways and gene ontology associations focused on Biological Processes, enrichment pathway analysis was conducted using the enrichGO function from the clusterProfiler R package.
